divergences.rule: Each is exercised by a corpus case carrying a divergence note, and reported by the external oracle as known rather than failed.

entries.case: same-width signed/unsigned ties resolve unsigned, both orders
entries.note: IEC does not define mixing signed with unsigned at all; our rule is that the UNSIGNED type wins the same-width tie, in either operand order, so the result is deterministic. (Bit strings no longer take part: arithmetic on ANY_BIT is rejected outright, which is what removed the other half of this divergence.)

entries.case: both operands of a BOOL AND are evaluated, so a guard does not protect a divide
entries.note: This engine evaluates both operands of a BOOL AND / OR, so the guarded divide faults. IEC leaves operand evaluation open, so implementations may differ: MATIEC stops at a decided operand, so this program returns FALSE there instead of faulting. A program whose behaviour depends on the difference is non-portable whichever way a simulator answers, so this engine answers the way that SURFACES it: a guard that silently worked here would stop a target that evaluates both operands.

entries.case: FOR evaluates bounds once and owns its iteration
entries.note: The loop bound is snapshotted at entry here, and BOTH independent IEC compilers whose behaviour could be inspected re-read it every iteration, so this program runs 3 times here and 10 times there. MATIEC: its generated C puts `if (I <= N)` inside the loop, reading the live variable. RuSTy (PLC-lang): its FOR lowering plants the user-written bound expression in the loop's exit test rather than a temporary, and says so in its own comment. Neither is provably right: IEC constrains FOR to a count "determined in advance", but no edition text reachable from here says WHEN the final-value expression is evaluated, so where to read it is this engine's own rule. Two compilers agreeing is weaker evidence than it looks, since both lower FOR to a C/LLVM-style loop where re-reading is the lazy path. The snapshot is kept anyway: it is what makes the iteration count knowable at entry, which is the property FOR exists for (WHILE is the construct for a condition re-tested each pass), and the only runaway guard here is a count rather than a clock (the interpreter faults a loop after 1,000,000 iterations), so a body that grows its own bound would run a million iterations in one scan before that fault stopped it. Because it cannot be settled, it is not left silent either: exporting a loop whose body writes its own bound now WARNS (export.ts), which is the honest response to a difference nobody can adjudicate.
the literal IEC F_TRIG body fires when CLK starts false; we suppress that startup pulse, since CLK was never TRUE before it

entries.case: SEL and MUX select; out-of-range MUX yields 0
entries.note: IEC declares an out-of-range MUX selector an error; we return 0

entries.case: REAL division by zero yields Infinity, not a fault
entries.note: float error handling is vendor-defined; REAL division by zero stays IEEE +/-Infinity here, matching PLC float hardware, which flags but does not fault. Only INTEGER division faults the scan

entries.case: an array index outside its bounds faults
entries.note: This engine faults on an array subscript outside its declared range. IEC requires a subscript to be within range but says nothing about what a runtime does when it is not, so faulting is a choice: this engine is where the mistake is cheapest to find. MATIEC does not check: it emits C, which reads past the array and completes the scan, so the replay reports "expected 0 scan lines, got 1" for this case.

entries.case: a store outside a subrange faults
entries.note: This engine faults on a store outside a subrange. IEC declares the range but leaves the runtime free, so faulting is this engine being the place the mistake is cheapest to find, exactly as with an array bound. MATIEC does not check and completes the scan, which is why the replay reports "expected 0 scan lines, got 1" here.

entries.case: an out-of-range length or position clamps instead of erroring
entries.note: IEC calls an out-of-range length/position an error. This engine clamps to the string instead - faulting a scan over a short string is not behaviour a controller survives.

IEC leaves float-to-text formatting to the implementation, and the vendors disagree (trailing zeros, exponent thresholds). We emit the shortest round-trip form. The VALUE is portable; the exact spelling is not, so do not parse it on the target.

entries.case: TIME_TO_STRING emits an IEC duration literal
entries.note: The output is an IEC duration literal (T#1s500ms); IEC does not fix a TIME_TO_STRING format. Chosen so the output round-trips back through STRING_TO_TIME.

entries.case: a fraction of a second prints in milliseconds, and a literal in a STRING reads back
entries.note: IEC fixes no spelling for a calendar value as text. A fraction of a second prints in milliseconds, three places; MATIEC prints six (TOD#07:05:09.500000). Text that is no date reads as 0 (1970-01-01, midnight), as STRING_TO_INT of text that is no number reads as 0.

entries.case: a TIME_OF_DAY pushed past midnight faults the scan
entries.note: This engine faults on a TOD result past 24:00:00, the same choice as for an array subscript or a subrange: the simulator is where the mistake is cheapest to find. MATIEC does not check a TOD result: it goes on past 24:00:00 with a value that is no time of day.

entries.case: a DATE_AND_TIME before 1970 faults the scan
entries.note: This engine's DT range is a 32-bit unsigned count of seconds from 1970, so it has no earlier instant, and a result before 1970 faults rather than hand a program a value an unsigned count cannot hold. MATIEC's count is signed and would go on.

This engine counts a TIME converted to a number in milliseconds, the unit TIME carries everywhere else. STruC++ (T#1500ms converts to 1500 in 0.6.2) counts the same. MATIEC counts WHOLE SECONDS (T#1500ms is 1), so a program that converts a TIME to a number reads a different number on a MATIEC target such as OpenPLC v3.

entries.case: DINT_TO_TIME and REAL_TO_TIME read the number as milliseconds
entries.note: MATIEC reads a number converted to a TIME as SECONDS (DINT_TO_TIME(1500) and REAL_TO_TIME(1500.0) are T#1500s), the mirror of its TIME_TO_DINT. This engine reads milliseconds (STruC++ 0.6.2 agrees), so a preset converted from a number lasts 1000 times longer on a MATIEC target such as OpenPLC v3.

entries.case: faults when a REF_TO that is NULL is dereferenced
entries.note: IEC 61131-3 makes dereferencing a NULL reference an error and leaves what a controller then does to the implementation. This engine faults the scan, naming it, as it faults a subscript out of range; STruC++'s runtime stops the POU the same way (its NullReference fault). MATIEC has no references

oracleCoverage.what: which accepted features an external IEC compiler has witnessed, at either of two grades: EXECUTED (compiled, stepped, and the variable image diffed against the golden scan for scan) or COMPILED ONLY (built by the 3rd-edition compiler but never run, because the 2nd-edition one refuses it by design)
oracleCoverage.why: the corpus SAMPLES the subset rather than covering it. "unverified" means unwitnessed by a real compiler, not known-broken - prefer the executed list where a program has the choice.

method.functionsAndBlocks: the engine's own lexer (valueRefs), so comments and string literals cannot count as coverage
method.types: whole-word match against case source with comments and string literals stripped - types are keywords, which the lexer does not emit as references
method.excluded: cases the oracle skips (never replayed) and `rejects` cases (they prove refusal, not behaviour)
method.grades: executed = replayed through MATIEC tier 2. compiledOnly = reached only by an `editionReject` case, which MATIEC is expected to refuse, so nothing ever ran it. Kept apart so the headline cannot drift upward on the weaker evidence as more editionReject cases accrue.
